title: 5T OTA
description: The five-transistor OTA, biased from the TAIL NODE and entered from the COMMON MODE. Internally the tail node is the one free bias variable: the pair's source sits at $V_{tail}$, so its body bias is $V_{tail}$, its drain-source voltage is $V_{out} - V_{tail}$, and every device is read straight out of the table with nothing iterated. The currents are stated the way the circuit sets them: only the bias reference is programmed, with $I_{tail}$; the tail device shares that reference's gate and width, so what it delivers is $I_{tail}$ less the mirror's drain-voltage error; the pair carries half of what the tail delivers; and the load mirror's output side shares its diode side's gate, so the two sides differ by their drain voltages in the same way. Held fixed and asked about at another process condition, the design therefore moves as the silicon would — one programmed current, with every other device following it through a shared gate or a shared node. Externally the designer types the common mode the application presents: $CM_{in} = V_{tail} + V_{GS}$ rises monotonically with the tail node, so the engine brackets $V_{tail}$ and bisects until the produced common mode equals $CM_{dc}$ — an inversion that cannot overshoot and owes nothing to a starting guess. Sweep $CM_{dc}$ to trace the common-mode axis. Gain falls as the common mode rises, because lifting the tail node squeezes the pair's own $v_{ds}$ — and it collapses well before the pair leaves saturation, which is why the gain rule, not a saturation edge, sets the usable ceiling.

params.name: vn_target
params.note: input-referred thermal density budget, set above the 28 nV/rtHz floor measured on a sky130 tt realization of this OTA rather than above the gamma-model row (22.7 nV/rtHz there at the default 20 uA and gm/ID split, the pair receiving a little under the programmed current). Clearing only the model is how a spec looks closable and is not; tighten this and the sweep shows what the noise really costs

params.name: vos_target
params.note: input offset budget, 1 sigma. Half-micron devices at 20 uA are SMALL (about 1.8 um x 0.5 um here), so the generic Pelgrom coefficient puts the spread near 9 mV — offset is the 5T's area tax, and shrinking this budget is what forces bigger devices. The systematic part is reported on its own row and is not charged against this budget

params.name: CM_lo
params.note: input CM range the application presents, low edge. The cm-lo edge re-evaluates the whole sheet here, so this claim is CHECKED at every evaluation, on the design this run produced — the sweep shows the widest range that would close (from 0.96 V up to the 1.45 V top of the CM_dc slider on sky130 tt at the shipped choices). The edge checks the ENDPOINT; the interior is the sweep's to show

params.name: CM_hi
params.note: input CM range the application presents, high edge — its ENDPOINT checked by the cm-hi edge the same way

params.name: CM_dc
params.note: the input common mode the application presents. The engine places the tail node so the sheet sits exactly here; sweep it to trace the common-mode axis

params.name: V_out_dc
params.note: output DC level; sets the mirror output device's vds and the top of the pair's own vds. The input device's drain and the mirror output device's drain meet at a high-impedance output that nothing on this sheet holds; the feedback the application closes around the amplifier holds it here. Wherever that is not one diode drop below the supply, the two sides of the load mirror carry different currents, and the systematic-offset row reports what that costs

params.name: avt
params.note: Pelgrom A_VT

params.name: abeta
params.note: Pelgrom A_beta

params.name: V_tail
params.note: the tail node — the design's one free bias variable, solved rather than set: the engine bisects between min and max (the BRACKET, not slider bounds) until the produced common mode equals CM_dc. It fixes the pair's body bias and drain-source voltage in one stroke; the shown value is where it landed. Both bracket ends must size: lowering V_out_dc below the max here leaves the pair no drain-source voltage at the high end, and the pin will say so

params.name: I_tail
params.note: the current the bias reference is programmed to — the one current on this sheet that is typed. The tail device mirrors it 1:1 through the shared gate and delivers it less the mirror's drain-voltage error (the tail node normally sits below the reference's diode drop); slew rate, bandwidth and supply current are computed from what is delivered, not from this number

params.name: gm_id_in
params.note: input-pair inversion: sets gm per current, noise, and the CM-low edge

params.name: gm_id_ld
params.note: mirror-load inversion, set on the diode side and inherited by the output side through the shared gate: lower gm/ID adds less noise and offset (both scale with the load's gm)

params.name: gm_id_tail
params.note: inversion level of the bias reference, which the tail device inherits through the shared gate: higher V* costs CM-low headroom

params.name: L_tail
params.note: length of the bias reference and of the tail device, which mirror at one length: longer shrinks the mirror's drain-voltage error

params.name: ld_sign
params.note: vds sign convention of the load table: +1 for an N-style axis, -1 for a signed-PMOS axis. Only the output side reads it — the diode side's drain follows its own gate in whichever convention its table uses. Read both sides of the mirror from the same table: the gate voltage they share is passed in that table's convention

doc.title: Tail bias reference
doc.description: The diode-connected reference the programmed current $I_{tail}$ flows into — the one device on this sheet whose current is typed. Its drain is its gate, so its $V_{DS}$ is its own $V_{GS}$ and the table is read along that diagonal with nothing estimated. It publishes its width and its gate voltage, which is all the tail device needs to copy it.

doc.title: Tail current source
doc.description: The tail device, on the bias reference's gate at the reference's width: a 1:1 mirror of the programmed current, with the tail node as its drain-source voltage. Its current is read off the table rather than typed — the reference sits at its own diode drop and this device at $V_{tail}$, so it delivers the programmed current scaled by what that difference in $V_{DS}$ does through its $g_{ds}$. It leaves saturation when $V_{tail}$ falls below its own $V_{dsat}$, which is what sets the low end of the usable common-mode range.

params.name: W_t
params.note: the bias reference's width — a 1:1 copy

params.name: vgs_t
params.note: the bias reference's gate voltage — the gate wire the two share

params.name: vds_t
params.note: the tail node

doc.title: Input-pair device
doc.description: Half-circuit input device at half the tail current, sized at the OUTPUT-side drain — the pair devices share a gate drive and a source but not a drain, and it is the output-side one whose $g_{ds}$ loads the gain. Both of its bias coordinates come from the tail node directly: the source sits at $V_{tail}$, so that is its body bias, and its drain-source voltage is what is left between the output level and that source.

doc.title: Mirror-load device, diode side
doc.description: The diode-connected side of the mirror load. It carries the current of the input device above it — half of what the tail delivers — and its drain is its gate, so it sits one $V_{GS}$ below the supply whatever the output does. That gate is the mirror node: this device's $g_m$ sets the second pole, and its width and gate voltage are what the output side copies.

doc.title: Mirror-load device, output side
doc.description: The output side of the mirror load, on the diode side's gate at the diode side's width. The output node and the supply set its drain, so the input common mode reaches it only through the small change in tail current that its diode side passes on, and its $g_{ds}$ is all but fixed once the output level is chosen. Its current is read off the table at that drain voltage rather than typed: wherever the output does not sit one diode drop below the supply it differs from the diode side's, and that difference is the systematic offset the sheet reports.

params.name: W_l
params.note: the diode side's width — a 1:1 copy

params.name: vgs_l
params.note: the diode side's gate voltage — the mirror node the two share, in the sign convention of the diode side's table

params.name: vds_l
params.note: output-side vds, signed to this table's axis convention

equations.name: CM_in
equations.note: the input common mode this bias produces — an OUTPUT here, not a setting. It rises monotonically with the tail node — which is why the pin that places the tail node from $CM_{dc}$ is a well-posed bisection

equations.name: Rout
equations.note: the resistance this OTA presents at its output — the two output-node conductances in parallel, both read at $V_{out,dc}$. The gain below assumes a capacitive load, so nothing here models a resistive one; this row is what a composing parent checks its own loading against

equations.name: Av
equations.note: half-circuit differential gain into the two output conductances, both read at the OUTPUT node $V_{out,dc}$ — the drain that actually loads the gain. Raising the tail node squeezes the pair's $v_{ds}$, so gain falls as the common mode rises

equations.name: f_pole
equations.note: estimate: the mirror-node pole, the diode side's $g_m$ over both mirror gates' $C_{GG}$; the 5T's second pole. Read on the diode side, the device whose $g_m$ is that node's conductance

equations.name: PM
equations.note: estimate: phase margin left after the mirror node. That node is a pole-ZERO DOUBLET, not a lone pole — only half the signal takes the mirror path, putting a zero at twice the pole — so it costs far less phase than $f_{pole}$ alone suggests

equations.name: SR
equations.note: the whole tail current steered into the load — the current the tail device delivers, not the number the reference is programmed to

equations.name: vn_in
equations.note: both pair devices and both mirror devices contribute, each at its own density: 2*vn_pair^2 + (vn_ldr*gm_ldr/gm_in)^2 + (vn_ld*gm_ld/gm_in)^2. The mirror's two sides are read separately because they sit at different drain voltages; counting all four devices is the simulation-verified two-sided total

equations.name: vos
equations.expr: sqrt(pelgrom_vos(avt, abeta, in__W, L_in, gm_id_in)^2 + (pelgrom_vos(avt, abeta, ldr__W, L_ld, gm_id_ld)*ldr__gm/in__gm)^2)
equations.note: random offset, 1 sigma: input-pair offset plus the mirror pair's offset referred by the gm ratio. The mirror pair is read at the diode side, whose width the output side copies

equations.name: vos_sys
equations.note: estimate: input-referred systematic offset. The mirror's output side shares the diode side's gate but sits at $V_{DD} - V_{out,dc}$ while the diode side sits at its own diode drop, so it asks for a different current than the half of the tail current the pair hands it. With $V_{out,dc}$ held by a loop outside this sheet, that difference has to come from an input imbalance of this size; it is zero when the output sits one diode drop below the supply. Reported only; no rule reads it

equations.name: tail_headroom
equations.note: how far the tail node sits above the tail device's saturation edge — exact here, because the tail node is the variable rather than something inferred from a common mode

equations.name: cgg_in
equations.note: estimate: the capacitance one input terminal presents — the gate capacitance of a single input device. Gate capacitance only, because the Miller term needs the gate-drain fraction and these tables do not carry it, so a driving stage sees more than this. No rule reads it

equations.name: I_q
equations.note: estimate: quiescent supply current of the amplifier — the current the tail device delivers is the whole of it, because the mirror load carries that same current down from the supply. The reference branch that programs it is shared bias infrastructure, typically one reference feeding several stages, and is not counted here. The datasheet line for comparing designs; no rule reads it

checks.note: estimate: margin left at crossover once the mirror doublet is paid for; advisory, since an open-loop OTA needs none of it and sim owns the real stability
computed from the gamma-model floor; this table carries no measured noise; the simulator owns noise sign-off
below this the tail source drops out of saturation and the bias current collapses; this is the mechanism behind the low end of the common-mode range
the common mode this bias produces has to sit inside the range the application presents
paired with cm-not-below. Sweep $CM_{dc}$ to see the whole span that closes — that span, not a saturation formula, is the common-mode range this design really supports

checks.justification: the pair's two drains sit at different levels — one a diode drop below the supply, the other at the output — and which is lower depends on V_out_dc, so this watches whichever it is. Gain collapses well before this trips, so treat it as a floor rather than as the usable ceiling
checks.note: trips when the tail node is pushed so high the pair runs out of drain-source voltage — lower V_tail, or spend less diode drop (lower gm_id_ld)

operatingRange.name: cm-lo
operatingRange.note: the claimed low edge, checked exactly: the whole sheet re-evaluates at CM_dc = CM_lo on the design this run produced — its own tail-node solve from the full bracket, every device held at the geometry it was sized to — and every hard rule must hold there. Replaces the linearized reach estimate this sheet used to carry

operatingRange.name: cm-hi
operatingRange.note: the claimed high edge, checked the same way. The edges check the ENDPOINTS; the interior is monotone for the saturation mechanisms here, and the CM_dc sweep remains the authority on the full landscape
